articles.title: Vikki Campion, News Corp columnist and wife of Barnaby Joyce, begins role with NSW One Nation
articles.summary:
Media adviser who married federal One Nation MP in 2023 confirms she has started working part-time for the party’s state executive

  • Get our

blocks.text: Vikki Campion, the News Corp columnist and wife of the federal One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, has begun working as an adviser for the party in New South Wales in the lead-up to the March state election.

Campion, who helped the NSW One Nation leader and candidate for Cessnock, Mike Newman, with a press conference in the Hunter electorate on Tuesday, told Guardian Australia she had started working for the party’s state executive as a contractor, providing media advice on a part-time basis this week.
She said it was “publicly disclosed that I [am] married to Barnaby on my website and the public are aware of my affiliation with One Nation through many media reports”.
“I’ve worked as a political contractor for around six years across a range of campaigns and candidates while writing regularly and running a farm,” she said.
“I report to the NSW state executive which is a separate entity to the federal One Nation, and I have previously worked for the state Nationals in similar arrangements.”
Campion writes a weekly column for the Saturday Telegraph, with her latest one published on 9 October.

Asked if she would disclose her work for the party in future columns for the paper, Campion said that “as an opinion writer, I don’t think anyone who has read my column would be shocked that I would want to help One Nation”.

After Guardian Australia put questions to the Daily Telegraph about Campion’s work with One Nation, the paper published an article about her new role in the party, which she told it was a “natural extension” of her career as a conservative commentator.
“Campion will continue to write her weekly column appearing every Saturday as a contributor,” the paper wrote.
After speaking to the Guardian, Campion subsequently posted to social media about her role, saying “the party is a phenomenon and unlike anything Australian politics has seen in a very long time”.

Campion worked as a media adviser to Joyce when he was deputy prime minister. The pair married in 2023. Joyce had announced in late 2017 that he and his first wife had separated and the Daily Telegraph subsequently published a photo of a pregnant Campion on its front page in February 2018.

In an appearance on the ABC’s Australian Story in August, Campion said she felt “suicidal” during a press conference called by the then prime minister, Malcolm Turnbull, after the story broke. The ABC issued an apology to Campion after the ABC News Instagram account published a clip from the episode with Campion discussing her experience of postpartum depression without disabling comments under the video.
after newsletter promotion
Joyce, the federal MP for New England, defected from the Nationals to One Nation last December.

The revelation about Campion’s work for the party came after News24 reported that another high-profile former Coalition figure, the 2022 Liberal candidate for Warringah, Katherine Deves, would run as an upper house candidate in the NSW election. Deves had previously announced that she joined One Nation in September.

But after News24 reported that Deves – who said she had received death threats after comments she had made about transgender people surfaced during the 2022 campaign – would run as an upper house candidate, One Nation put out a statement saying it had only confirmed three candidates – Newman and the upper house candidates Stuart Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer based in Tamworth.

“We have received more than 800 [candidate] applications from community leaders, advocates and business people,” a spokesperson said. Campion told Guardian Australia she had no plans to run as a candidate for the party.
One Nation and the Saturday Telegraph were contacted for comment.

articles.title: Bullet hole in door and DNA evidence scrutinised in Beau Lamarre-Condon double murder trial
articles.summary:
Defence also cross-examines witness over postmortem examinations of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: A bullet hole left in a bedroom door and DNA found in the barrel of the firearm have been scrutinised in court as Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial continues in Sydney.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

The prosecution argues the policeman disguised himself as an UberEats rider before entering Baird’s home, shooting him twice – in the base of the neck and the right temple – and then shooting Davies through the bedroom door.

But the defence alleges they were killed in two separate incidents when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”. During the tussle with Baird, the firearm was flung across the room where it was picked up by Davies, who later shot himself in a struggle with the policeman, the defence argues.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC cross-examined crime scene officer Greg Moon on Tuesday, questioning the prosecution’s version of events.

Stratton pointed to a swab taken from the barrel of the alleged murder weapon, which returned a DNA profile that partially matched Davies. He then noted the hole in the bedroom door, through which the prosecution alleges Davies was shot, tested negative for blood.

Stratton suggested: “The possibility or likelihood of biological material finding its way from a wound of the deceased through a hole in the door less than a centimetre in width and into the barrel of a gun … approaches zero.”
But Moon told the New South Wales supreme court he disagreed.
“I believe it can still happen,” he said.
The defence does not dispute the couple were shot.
A diagram from Dr Kendall Bailey, who conducted the postmortem examinations of both men, suggested a bullet entered Baird’s body at the base of his neck and exited just below his lip.
Asked by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about the effect of this wound, Bailey told the jury it did not pass through any major vessels of the neck or the vertebral column or windpipe.
But that did not mean it was insignificant, the court heard.
“It still would be a very nasty injury and that fracturing of the jaw is a very nasty injury,” she told the court.
While it is potentially survivable, those kinds of injuries can be painful and cause some to pass out, though others may not lose consciousness, Bailey explained.
Hatfield then asked if person with those injuries could speak.
after newsletter promotion
The bullet went through the jaw and the base of the tongue, Bailey said, adding: “I don’t think anyone with that injury would be making any meaningful vocalisations.
“They could make a noise but that would be nothing that would be coherent,” she said.
Bailey then explained the shot that entered the temple would go through the brain, where it would incapacitate a person.

Asked if that person would then be able to fling a gun to the other side of the room, she said the body could make some involuntary movements but “I don’t think that person is making any conscious movements”.
CT scans of Baird and Davies’ skulls showing the damage caused by the bullets were presented to the jury on Thursday.

Forensic radiologist Dr James Raleigh explained to the court there was a hole in the right side of Baird’s head at the temple region and multiple small bone fragments “presumably from that damage were run in a line across the inside of the skull”.
Davies’ wound was located in his face just above the left eyebrow, which Raleigh agreed was consistent with a bullet hole.
Two wounds on Davies’ thigh were consistent with a “single-bladed weapon”, Bailey said.
But she agreed those injuries likely took place after or at the time of death.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: US immigration authorities raid home of Democratic Trump critic Ilhan Omar
articles.summary: The raid on the home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota occurs a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump's party seeking to retain control of Congress

items: US authorities conducted a predawn raid on the home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud related to her family's immigration paperwork.
Omar claims the raid is politically motivated and part of a campaign of intimidation by President Trump, who has targeted her with insults and accusations over the years.

Democratic leaders have condemned the raid as an abuse of power, while some Republicans argue that if fraud is proven, Omar should face consequences, highlighting the ongoing political tensions ahead of the midterm elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – US authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday, October 12, on the Washington, DC, home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said.

A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar said. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”
Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar, 44, is seeking a fifth two-year term in the US House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3.
Campaigning in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump quickly turned to Omar, who was born in Somalia and became a US citizen in 2000, settling in Minnesota, home to a large community of Somalis.
“She comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” Trump said. “What a mess they have done — Somalia.“
The crowd chanted: “Deport, deport.”
He urged supporters to vote Republican “if you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked, and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed.”

In announcing the raid, a Justice Department spokesperson said: “Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation.”
Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that “something’s gonna happen” in the investigation into Omar’s family’s entry into the United States.
“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time.

Monday’s raid occurred a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump’s party seeking to retain control of Congress. Omar, a prominent progressive, represents a safe Democratic district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.

Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect an election’s outcome or benefit a candidate or party. It historically has avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election.

In a statement, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party’s leadership in the chamber said the raid was “deeply disturbing and raises serious questions” about the weaponization of the federal government against Trump’s enemies.

Republicans have “relentlessly targeted” Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family,” they added, and they vowed to “deliver full accountability” for a “rogue abuse of power.”
Minnesota Democrats also condemned the raid.
“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota Governor Tim Walz wrote on social media. “President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”

Few Republican lawmakers publicly commented. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote online: “If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and removed from this country. NO ONE is above the law.”

George Washington University law professor Randall Eliason, a former US public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appears to be a break with past Justice Department practice of avoiding investigative steps likely to become public close to Election Day. But Eliason noted there is no way of enforcing the policy.

“The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process,” Eliason said. “It’s not surprising that they wouldn’t really care about violating this policy because they’ve shown they don’t really care about politicizing the Justice Department in many other ways.”

A person familiar with the investigation said the Justice Department consulted with its Public Integrity Section, a unit that has historically advised and approved investigations of members of Congress, and acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter prior to the search. The Trump administration has reduced the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers and curtailed much of its authority.
The Justice Department during Trump’s second term in office has investigated and brought charges against a range of Trump’s perceived political enemies.

It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney General Letitia James and Trump’s former national security adviser-turned-critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.

The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes.

Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has cast the Somali-American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump’s focus on her an “unhealthy and creepy obsession.”
Civil rights advocates have criticized Trump’s rhetoric toward ​minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis “garbage.”
Omar has said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to “hateful political rhetoric,” especially from Trump.

Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar was sentenced to ​14 months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he ​disagreed with her progressive views. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sandiganbayan slaps Jinggoy Estrada with new 90-day suspension order
articles.summary: The anti-graft court orders a copy of the ruling served on the office of Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian for implementation

blocks.text: JINGGOY. Senator Jinggoy Estrada, in a yellow detainee uniform and handcuffs, arrive at the Sandiganbayan anti-graft court in Quezon City on June 4, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for his alleged graft case related to government flood control projects.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The anti-graft court orders a copy of the ruling served on the office of Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian for implementation

items: Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been placed under a second 90-day preventive suspension by the Sandiganbayan anti-graft court due to a flood control projects scandal, despite having completed a previous suspension.

The court's decision, signed by three associate justices, mandates the suspension to be implemented by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and comes as Estrada's defense continues to contest the charges against him.

The 5th Division of the court is handling plunder and graft charges against Estrada and several suspended Department of Public Works and Highways officials, with the court emphasizing that preventive suspension is mandatory when valid charges are filed.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The suspension of Senator Jinggoy Estrada was supposed to be over. He had completed 90 days out of office under an earlier order, a measure tied to a pending graft case.
But late Monday, October 12, the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan delivered another order, placing him under a second 90-day preventive suspension in the flood control projects scandal.
The anti-graft court ordered a copy of the ruling served on the office of Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian for implementation.

The decision, issued by the anti-graft court’s 5th Division, put the senator back under a legal cloud even as his defense continued to contest the charges against him. It was signed by Associate Justices Zaldy Trespeses, Maryann Corpus-Mañalac, and Gener Gito.
Estrada completed a 90-day suspension ordered by the Sandiganbayan’s 2nd Division in June in connection with a pending case under the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.

The 5th Division is hearing the plunder and second graft charges against Estrada and three suspended Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials: South Manila district engineer Manny Bulusan, North Manila assistant district engineer Denryl Caesar Cortuna, and Quezon City 1st district engineer Arturo Gonzales.

Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan, who was initially charged along with them, was dropped from the cases before the 5th Division at the prosecution’s request after offering to testify for the government.

“Accused Senator Jose ‘Jinggoy’ P. Ejercito Estrada Estrada is suspended from his position as Senator of the Republic of the Philippines and from any other public office which he may now or hereafter be holding for a period of ninety (90) days from receipt of this Resolution,” read part of the Sandiganbayan division ruling.

The three DPWH officials had been suspended since June 29, after they were arraigned before Estrada and Bonoan. The senator and the former secretary had challenged the validity of the charges through motions to quash.
Estrada was arraigned on September 3 but declined to enter a plea, leading the court to enter a not-guilty plea on his behalf.

His lawyers challenged the second suspension, arguing that the validity of the indictment had yet to be resolved, that his detention without bail meant he could no longer interfere with the prosecution, and that another suspension would amount to punishment rather than a preventive measure.

The 5th Division cited jurisprudence establishing preventive suspension as mandatory when a valid information has been filed for violation of the anti-graft law. It also noted the requirement for a pre-suspension hearing.
“With the court’s disposition of all incidents relating to the validity of the information against him, his preventive suspension is now in order,” the court stated. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion, witness says
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion from 2022 to 2025, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera told the impeachment court on Monday, October 12,…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 10:21am

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion from 2022 to 2025, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera told the impeachment court on Monday, October 12, citing potential discrepancies in financial records and income from business interests.
The estimate is nearly double the P817.87 million in unexplained wealth Cabrera had previously calculated, based on his review of Duterte’s financial records.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero asked Cabrera how much Duterte’s undeclared wealth could reach if he had not used conservative assumptions in his analysis.

“Kung hindi po kayo conservative, kung ito po 'yung bare minimum, in your expertise and based on your review of the documents, ano po ba 'yung sukdulang hangganan? Kung ito po 'yung bare minimum niyo, ano po 'yung inyong maximum?” Escudero asked.

(If you were not being conservative and this is the bare minimum, based on your expertise and review of the documents, what would be the upper limit? If this is your bare minimum, what would be your maximum?)
(Based lang po sa mga documents po na nakita namin, hindi ko po sinama ang confidential funds po. So 475 (million) po ’yun,” Cabrera said.
(Based only on the documents we reviewed, I did not include the confidential funds. So that would be P475 million.)

He added that discrepancies involving the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) could amount to P100 million if he did not use conservative assumptions. Applying a 45% assumption used for GenCorp Industries Inc. to undeclared sales could also increase the estimated amount by around P250 million.
Cabrera said these adjustments could nearly double his initial estimate.
“Mga 1.5 po,” he told Escudero when asked to compute the maximum estimate.
“1.5 billion?” Escudero asked.
“1.5 billion po,” Cabrera replied, clarifying that the amount was less than P1.6 billion.
Escudero then confirmed whether the P1.5-billion figure represented the maximum estimate of Duterte’s undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025, without double-counting amounts across different years.
“Tama po,” Cabrera said. (That’s correct.)
Business interests account for part of estimate

During the hearing, Escudero also examined how much of Cabrera’s initial P817.87-million estimate would remain if income attributed to Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, from their business interests were excluded.
These included GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro Chow King Foods and Cale 88 Food Corp.
Escudero cited Cabrera’s computation that GenCorp accounted for approximately 25.9% of the total, equivalent to P212.63 million.
He also cited the combined P142.2 million attributed to Metro Chow King Foods and Cale 88 Food Corp., equivalent to 17.3% of the estimated unexplained wealth.

Escudero said that excluding the amounts attributed to GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and Cale 88 Foods Corp. would leave P463.05 million in unexplained wealth, based on Cabrera’s review of bank accounts and insurance policies.
The amount represents 56.6% of his initial P817.87-million estimate, which Cabrera affirmed.
Tax liabilities may reduce total
Escudero also asked whether taxes that should have been paid on the wealth would have to be deducted from the estimate.
Cabrera said this was possible, explaining that any outstanding tax liability could be subtracted when calculating the amount.
“Whether it's the low of 817 (million) or the high of 1.5 (billion), any liability would have to be subtracted or deducted from that?” Escudero asked
“Tama po,” Cabrera replied. (That’s correct.)
Cabrera explained that the classification of wealth as unexplained depended not only on whether its source was known but also on whether the source was legal.
“Pero ’pag ang pinanggalingan po ay hindi po legal, nagiging unexplained din po siya kahit alam niyo po kung saan nanggaling,” he said
(But if the source is illegal, it also becomes unexplained wealth, even if you know where it came from.)

Cabrera was presented by the prosecution as an expert witness on Article II of the impeachment complaint against Duterte, which accuses the vice president of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income, failing to fully disclose her assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and maintaining prohibited business interests while in office.

articles.title: ‘Clear and present danger’: fuel prices could rise by 30c a litre across Australia under IMF scenario
articles.summary:
IMF’s World Economic Outlook shows how a worsening Middle East crisis could affect global growth and inflation

An International Monetary Fund scenario where global oil prices jump to US$130…

blocks.text: An International Monetary Fund scenario where global oil prices jump to US$130 a barrel over coming months could push Australian petrol prices up by another 30 cents per litre and pile pressure on the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates, economists say.

In its latest World Economic Outlook, the IMF modelled the impact on global growth and inflation from a worsening Middle East crisis that extended into next year, highlighting the “clear and present danger” to a resilient global economy from turmoil in commodity and bond markets.
The Washington-based institution did not publish the impact on Australia from a hypothetical US$30 jump in the price of crude oil, from over US$106 a barrel now.

The IMF described a scenario where “the conflict persists through the end of June 2027, keeping the straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb largely closed to commercial shipping, extending damages to oil infrastructures in the region, and delaying the recovery in oil supply to the end of 2027”.
“With limited scope for further inventory drawdown, oil prices reach $US130 from the fourth quarter of 2026 to the first quarter of 2027.”

Unleaded petrol prices in the major east coast cities have pushed above $2.40 a litre in recent days and towards six-month highs, while diesel prices have eased but remain high at about $2.80 per litre.

Using a rule of thumb that every US$10 rise in global oil prices leads to a 10c price rise at the bowser, a US$30 oil price increase could drive unleaded petrol towards $2.70 and the highest since the start of the war more than seven months ago.

Economists told Guardian Australia that such a move could leave inflation more than 1 percentage point higher than expected by the end of the year, adding to households’ cost of living woes and dragging on growth.
Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “the reality” was that the RBA – alongside other central banks – would have to respond to higher fuel costs with higher interest rates.
“The question is how much higher,” Kearns said.

The RBA delivered a fourth interest rate hike last month. Minutes from that meeting released on Tuesday showed that board members discussed how “the Middle East conflict had escalated and oil prices were substantially above the level assumed in the August forecasts”.
“More broadly, members noted that global cost pressures appeared to be building. Some of this came from the indirect effects of higher oil prices,” the minutes read.
Johnathan McMenamin, head of economic forecasts at Barrenjoey, said he expected inflation to lift to 4.2% in the year to September, against 4% in August.
McMenamin said that every 10% rise in fuel prices directly added 0.33 percentage points to headline inflation.
The RBA’s prediction of a fall in headline inflation to 3.6% by the end of the year is based on the Brent crude price falling to US$81 per barrel.

Should global oil prices instead push towards US$130 per barrel, as per the IMF scenario (and assuming each US$10 oil price increase leads to a 10c rise in fuel prices), inflation could instead still be as high as 4.5% in late 2026.

But McMenamin was less convinced the RBA would have to respond with higher interest rates, saying the central bank has been mostly responding to underlying price pressures related to domestic capacity constraints, rather than overseas factors.

articles.title: Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
articles.summary: Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of October

blocks.text: ROAD TO AIRPORT. General view of the highway leading to the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 12, 2026.
Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of October

items: Riyadh's international airport closure has been extended until October 17 due to ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis, leading to widespread flight cancellations.
The attacks, including a ballistic missile strike on the airport, have resulted in significant casualties and raised concerns about the safety of civil aviation in the region.
Airlines globally are suspending services to Saudi Arabia, with the disruptions impacting the country's economy and scheduled events, including major conferences.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh’s international airport until Saturday, October 17, and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia’s capital.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities,” the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

Late on Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.
The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom’s southwest with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
A Notice to Airmen issued on Monday showed King Khalid International Airport will stay closed until 2100 GMT on October 17.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.
They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.
“This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice.
“I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully,” he said.
Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country’s west coast.
Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia. EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Friday, citing missile and drone attacks.
“The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.
OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia.
That adds “extensive distance” for some routes and “closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers,” Zee said.
Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month.

Etihad Airways said it had canceled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption,” adding that all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would be canceled until October 19.
Qatar Airways said on Monday it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the “current situation.”
Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on October 23, until March 2027.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the program. – Rappler.com

articles.title: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
articles.summary: World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026

blocks.text: The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.
It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.

However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.

“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”

The International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, and promised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month.
But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.

Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, which analysts said would have little “meaningful” effect.

The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank are holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.

Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged governments to tighten their belts, amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.
In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.
US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.

The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July – in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is set to arrive in Bangkok later this week.

However, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
after newsletter promotion

However, the IMF warned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.
“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.
Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.
The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.
Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.

The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.
As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies owning properties linked to her by NBI
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday denied ownership of the properties being investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) that were supposedly linked to her and her family.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 9:53am
Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday denied ownership of the properties being investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) that were supposedly linked to her and her family.
In a statement, the Vice President raised concern about the move of the NBI to associate the properties to her, calling it a kind of “public deception.”

“Nakakabahala na ang National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), na pinopondohan ng taumbayan, ay ginagamit ang kanilang mga operasyon para sa mga gawaing walang malinaw na pakinabang sa publiko,” she said.
(It is alarming that the National Bureau of Investigation, an agency funded by the people, is utilizing its operations for activities that offer no clear public benefit.)
“Ang lote sa larawan na sinabi niyang nasa aking Statement of Assets, Liability, and Net Worth o SALN ay hindi sa akin,” she added.
(The lot shown in the photograph, which was claimed to be listed in my Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, does not belong to me.)
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said that the agency is investigating the properties to follow a pattern supposedly established in the affidavit of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

To recall, Gracioso had claimed that he delivered cash to the Vice President, Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
The Dutertes have denied the claims of Gracioso. Velasco’s camp also previously said the allegations against him had “no basis.”
Matibag said Gracioso’s affidavit pointed to a pattern of “land banking” among properties linked to the Velasco family, which the NBI was now examining in connection with the Dutertes.
But the Vice President argued that the evidence presented by the NBI was “questionable.”

“Ang ganitong panlilinlang sa publiko ay ang dahilan kung bakit inalis ang NBI sa listahan ng mga testigong ihaharap ng prosekusyon sa impeachment proceedings—dahil sa mga alegasyon na muli na naman silang naglahad ng mga ebidensiyang kuwestiyonable tulad noong Gracioso affidavit,” she said.

(This kind of public deception is the reason why the NBI was removed from the prosecution's list of witnesses for the impeachment proceedings—because of the allegations wherein they presented questionable evidence, much like in Gracioso’s affidavit.)

“Kung pera ng taumbayan ang ginagamit sa pagpapatakbo ng isang ahensiya, nararapat lamang na tiyakin na ang bawat hakbang nito ay naaayon sa batas, nakabatay sa katotohanan, at nagsisilbi sa interes ng sambayanan,” she continued.
(When public funds are used to operate an agency, it is only right to ensure that every action taken is lawful, grounded in truth, and serves the interests of the people.)
The properties that the NBI linked to the Vice President were presented in the impeachment trial on Monday, during the interjection of Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: P41-million withdrawal from Mans Carpio’s accounts in 73 minutes ‘unusual' — witness
articles.summary: A forensic accountant has described as “unusual” the withdrawal of P41 million in cash from the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Mans Carpio, within an hour and 13…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 9:13am

MANILA, Philippines — A forensic accountant has described as “unusual” the withdrawal of P41 million in cash from the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Mans Carpio, within an hour and 13 minutes on Aug. 6, 2024, saying the closely timed transactions appeared rushed.

Responding to Sen. Risa Hontiveros’ questions during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, October 12, forensic accountant Alexander Cabrera said the amount and timing of the withdrawals raised questions.
“Sa ordinaryong tao po, unusual po. Eh 41 million in cash, kailangan n'yo po siyempre ng bag po doon. And parang may hinahabol po eh, kasi lahat po ginawa within the hour po,” he said.
(For an ordinary person, that would be unusual. P41 million in cash would, of course, require a bag to carry. And it seemed like they were in a hurry because everything was done within an hour.)
Hontiveros cited Table 24, page 18 of Cabrera’s forensic report, which recorded the total cash withdrawals of P41 million on Aug. 6, 2024.

Cabrera confirmed that both accounts involved in the transactions belonged to Carpio. He questioned why such a large amount was withdrawn in cash instead of being transferred to another bank account or obtained through a manager’s check.
He said the absence of supporting documents could also serve as evidence in a forensic investigation, particularly when a transaction took place without a clear paper trail.

“Pagka po ‘yung mga transactions po kulang sa trail, kulang sa record, wala pong document evidencing it pero nangyari po yung transaction, yung pong walang document nangyari yung transaction, evidence din po ‘yun eh,” Cabrera said.
(When transactions lack a trail, lack records and have no documents to support them, but the transactions still took place, the absence of documentation is also evidence.)
His team also examined the timestamps of the withdrawals and found that the transactions were closely spaced, with the final withdrawal taking place after a lunch break.
“Nag-lunch muna, tapos kinuha po ‘yun. Kaya sabi namin parang may hinahabol kasi right after lunch tuloy ‘yung transaction. Matagal din po kasi magbilang ng 41 million,” he said.

(They [Carpio's camp] had lunch first, then withdrew the money. That’s why we said it seemed like they were in a hurry because the transaction continued right after lunch. It also takes a long time to count P41 million.)
Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, meanwhile, questioned the timing of the withdrawals in relation to developments involving Duterte and Carpio.

"'Yung August 6, 2024, sabi ninyo 41 million ang winithdraw sa isang araw at parang may hinahabol. So ako rin naging curious dito, kaya iniisip ko, ano ba nangyari noong August 6 o kaya thereabouts, no?" Pangilinan said.

(On August 6, 2024, you said P41 million was withdrawn in a single day and that it seemed like someone was in a hurry. I became curious about this too so I wondered what happened on August 6 or around that time.)
He noted that Duterte resigned as education secretary on July 19, 2024, before drug charges were filed against Carpio on July 30 in connection with the so-called magnetic lifter case.

Just to place on record, uh, Vice President Sara Duterte resigned as DepEd chairperson July 19, 2024. And then on July 30, uh, it's in the news and we can Google it because that's what we did, uh, drug charges were filed against Attorney Mans Carpio doon sa, um, 'yong tawag dito, magnetic lifter," Pangilinan said.
"So July 30 'yun. So that was, uh, the filing was July 30, and then six days later nangyari ito," he added, referring to the August 6 withdrawals.
(So that was on July 30. The charges were filed on July 30, and then this happened six days later.)

Carpio has maintained that the credit card expenses discussed during the impeachment trial were personal expenditures paid for with his own money. He has also denied Duterte's involvement in the transactions and said no public funds were used.

Cabrera was presented by the prosecution as an expert witness on Article II of the impeachment complaint against Duterte, which accuses the vice president of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income, failing to fully disclose her assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and maintaining prohibited business interests while in office.

articles.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte dies
articles.summary: RJ Mitte said his lived experience with cerebral palsy was an asset for his role as Walter White's son Flynn on "Breaking Bad."

image.caption: RJ Mitte had key roles in 'Breaking Bad,' 'Switched at Birth' and 'Guardians of Justice'Image: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: American actor RJ Mitte, whose lived experience with cerebral palsy was channeled into a key role in "Breaking Bad," died on Monday at the age of 34.
"It is with profound ​sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights ​advocate RJ Mitte," his management agency said in a statement.
No other details about the circumstances of his death were given.

In addition to his breakout role in in "Breaking Bad" and later credits including "Switched at Birth" and "Guardians of Justice," Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Hospitals for Children.
An 'authentic' breakout role

In "Breaking Bad," Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston's character, chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White. Mitte's character used crutches and spoke with a slur, and gained greater prominence as the series progressed.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built ​a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said.
"Breaking Bad" ran from 2008 until 2023. With 16 Emmy awards, it's often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time.

Shortly after the series wrapped up, Mitte told the Associated Press that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all of which featured in the show — made him better in his role.
"You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," he said in 2024.
"You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder," Mitte added.

articles.title: Supreme Court orders release of mining tycoon Joseph Sy amid citizenship dispute
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has ordered the release of Globe-Ferronickel chairman Joseph Sy.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 8:22am
Joseph Sy attends the Senate inquiry on Dec. 15, 2025 which tackled the alleged abuse of identity documents reserved to Filipino citizens by foreign nationals.
Senate of the Philippines - Social Media Unit
MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has ordered the release of Globe-Ferronickel chairman Joseph Sy.
In a resolution dated October 7, the high court granted a writ of preliminary mandatory injunction.
According to a copy of the order obtained by Philstar.com, the order took effect upon the posting of a P900,000.00 cash bond.
On Aug. 21, 2025, Sy was intercepted and detained by Bureau of Immigration personnel at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) upon his arrival from Hong Kong.

The bureau acted on a mission order issued by Immigration Commissioner Joel Viado, claiming that Sy was an alias for Zhong Zhen Chen, a Chinese national who had allegedly misrepresented himself as a Filipino.

To support their claim, immigration officials presented fingerprint evidence from an Alien Certificate of Registration issued 29 years ago, which they said matched the fingerprints on Sy's Philippine passport.
However, Sy’s representative, Dante Bravo, filed a petition for habeas corpus, arguing that Sy is a Filipino citizen.
Bravo provided Sy's Certificate of Live Birth, issued through late registration in 2007, which identifies him as a Filipino born in Quezon City to Filipino parents.
Sy also holds a Philippine passport valid until 2031 and various other government identification cards.

On February 20, the Court of Appeals ruled that Sy’s continued detention was unlawful, finding that the Bureau of Immigration cannot institute summary deportation proceedings against someone with a valid birth certificate.
In a statement, the Bureau of Immigration said that it would respect the Supreme Court’s decision.
However, the bureau emphasized that Sy's release from custody does not “constitute a final determination of the questions surrounding his citizenship and identity.”

“It is also noted that the case before the Supreme Court is an appeal in the Habeas Corpus Petition involving Mr. Sy, which only involves questions on legality of his detention, and not a determination on his citizenship,” the Bureau of Immigration’s statement read.
“The Bureau acted in the exercise of its statutory mandate to investigate questions concerning immigration status, identity, and citizenship documentation,” it added.

articles.title: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case

image.caption: The FBI arrested a 'suspected co-conspirator' in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov, who Reuters and court records have identified as Canadian cybersecurity expert Ed Dubrovsky. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada
Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear a prominent ransomware negotiator was arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.
The prominent ransomware negotiator was arrested last week
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 12, 2026 8:10 PM EDT | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago

Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear that a prominent ransomware negotiator had been arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.
FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday confirmed the arrest of a "suspected co-conspirator" in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov which exposed a trove of sensitive data about FBI staff.
"We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," Patel said on social media.

Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers.

Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.
The allegations have not been proven in court.

FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during a Senate Judiciary hearing on Oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in September 2026 in Washington. Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters investigation. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)
'A sense of shock'
"For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday.
Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened."
"This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well."

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
Dutch police arrest security professional in ShinyHunters investigation

blocks.text: The ​court records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of the suspect's last ⁠name — "Dobrovsky" or "Dobrosky" — and do not identify his age, profession or employer.
Prison records show a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is being held at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

Reuters reported that electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a 54-year-old resident of Richmond Hill, a suburb of Toronto.
Long history in cybersecurity

Dubrovsky's LinkedIn profile describes him as a specialist in ‌negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments, as well as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert, business leader, speaker, author and educator."
According to his profile, Dubrovsky has held senior positions in cybersecurity for decades.

He wrote on LinkedIn last month that he would be attending the NetDilligence conference in Philadelphia in October with cybersecurity firm CyberSteward. The company posted photos of Dubrovsky at the conference a week ago and said he was signing copies of a book he recently published about handling cyber extortion.
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter

In the book's introduction, Dubrovsky writes: "I have negotiated with criminals who viewed themselves as martyrs, criminal masterminds, and patriots of their own countries even after deploying malware against critical infrastructure and causing billions of dollars in damage. Such people could still look in the mirror and see goodness."
CBC News reached out to CyberSteward by phone, email and in person at its Toronto address, but did not get a response Monday.
The FBI's national press office declined to comment directly on Dubrovsky's arrest and referred CBC News to Patel's statement.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon told The Canadian Press on Friday that "the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack," but directed all further questions to the FBI.
ShinyHunters 'poked the bear': expert
ShinyHunters is known as one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups, typically demanding ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it has obtained.

The hacking group caused chaos at universities around the world in May, including in Canada, with a cyberattack on Canvas, an online learning-management system that connects millions of students with their instructors.
ShinyHunters has also been associated with high-profile cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, Ticketmaster, Pornhub and Rockstar Games.

items: What drives ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for hacking the FBI?

blocks.text: Last month, the group claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — in what it said was retaliation for the law enforcement agency making false claims about the group.
ShinyHunters later told CBC News they would not release the data.

David Shipley, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of Fredericton-based Beauceron Security, said the stunt "poked the bear" and has "literally unleashed the most powerful law enforcement agency in the world on them."
Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight
Shipley said surprise was the first thing that came to mind when he heard of the latest arrest.
"I knew the ShinyHunters investigation was going to go in interesting places because it's already the stuff of Hollywood movies," he told CBC News.
"I don't think anyone saw this twist coming."
Shipley said Dubrovsky was well regarded and worked for "top-tier" cybersecurity firms.
"I feel terrible for his former colleagues, both at his current firm and his past firms, who have been dragged through these awful headlines," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.

articles.title: One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US
articles.summary:
Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop

One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a…

blocks.text: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.
The incident took place a Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department.

Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citing eyewitnesses and anonymous local officials.
The rollercoaster, which was introduced at the park in 2006, has a top speed of 70mph (110km/h) and a 175ft drop.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.

Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week.

articles.title: English councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028
articles.summary:
Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of support

Councils are warning of potentially “catastrophic” debts, which are forecast to reach…

blocks.text: Councils are warning of potentially “catastrophic” debts, which are forecast to reach a record £10bn over the next 18 months, as a result of rapid growth in demand for special educational needs and disability (Send) support in English schools.

Although the government recently cleared more than £5bn in historic council Send debts, a surge in requests has led to authorities predicting they will have re-accrued that debt figure by April, and doubled it by 2028.

The recent acceleration in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which mandate support for conditions such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD, is thought to partly reflect a rush by parents and schools to secure support before the government’s changes to Send provision take effect.

The prospect of council finances being overwhelmed by schools’ Send spending reflects similar concerns in the NHS and the benefit system over the strain the rising prevalence of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions has put on public services.

The government-commissioned Fonagy report, published last week, found the increase in these conditions was real and a cause of distress to many who have them, but the resulting demand for support would be unsustainable without introducing new ways to manage the pressure on public services.

The County Councils Network (CCN), which published the forecasts on Tuesday, said the overspending was not the fault of councils and called on ministers to guarantee future Send debts run up by local authorities, some of whom would be otherwise left effectively bankrupt as a result of meeting their legal duties.

Linden Kemkaran, the CCN’s Send spokesperson, said: “These deficits have not accumulated because councils have chosen to spend recklessly: they are the result of having to meet rapidly growing statutory demand, which has only intensified this year, without funding keeping pace.

“If councils are left carrying billions of pounds of Send debt, it will not just be a problem for local authorities. Taxpayers and local communities will ultimately bear the consequences as councils face impossible choices about how to protect frontline services while managing debts that have accrued through no fault of their own.

She added: “As well as councils absorbing skyrocketing costs, children and young people will face increasingly long waits for support and educational outcomes will continue to flatline. New ministers now need to provide certainty that they will deliver the full package of reforms needed to ensure the system works much better for young people, schools and councils.”

The government’s reforms aim to gradually replace the current system in England with a more inclusive approach of Send support in mainstream schools that in principle obviates the need for an EHCP. However, parents appear to be rushing to secure formal support now to avoid any future uncertainty.

Without a ministerial guarantee to wipe future overspending, councils say they are at risk of bankruptcy when those accumulated debts – currently kept off town hall balance sheets under a special “override” arrangement with the Treasury – go back on to the books in April 2028 when the override is due to expire.

Ministers have agreed to pay 90% of English top tier councils’ Send debts accumulated to March 2026, but it is unclear how far future Send debts will be covered. Ministers have previously said future debt support would be “appropriate and proportionate” but that it would “not be unlimited”.

The CCN said anything less than a ministerial commitment to pay down 90% of future Send debt would be a “financial catastrophe” for councils – and some authorities would struggle with solvency even if they retained just 10% of their Send debts.

Publicly available internal reports by local authorities show a number are predicting overspends of more than £100m in 2026-27 alone. Hampshire county council is forecasting a £200m deficit for this year. Others include Surrey, East Sussex, Kent, Worcestershire and Norfolk county councils.

The EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools.

In January, the number of young people with EHCPs reached 718,000, after a 12.5% increase over the past 12 months. This was the largest year on year increase since the plans were introduced in 2014. An additional 1.3 million young people have identified special needs, according to official data.

Many councils are anticipating annual double digit increases over the next three years, with several now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.

The Fonagy report said the growth in EHCPs had “substantially outpaced the capacity” of the education system to respond. Of the 105,300 statutory assessments carried out in 2024, 94% resulted in the award of an EHCP.

Owen Mapley, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said: “The continued escalation of Send deficits exposes a serious failure to align statutory responsibilities with funding levels. Local government chief financial officers have been calling attention to this disconnect for years as it undermines proper financial management practice.”

A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain, and have always recognised that both deficits and EHCP applications will continue to rise before our reforms are fully rolled out.

“On top of grants to pay off 90% of council deficits, we’re investing billions to make sure every community has easy, early access to specialists like speech and language therapists, and so councils can deliver their tailored local reform plans.
“Fixing the Send system will take time and councils will need further support with deficits, so we will set out the details before March 2028.”

articles.title: 2 Filipinos under probe over Laos shabu haul bound for PH — PDEA
articles.summary: The agency said they are currently building a case against the two Filipinos, noting that some of the information remains confidential amid the probe.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 6:54am
Motorists drive past Laos national flags and Lao People's Revolutionary Party flags ahead of the election in Vientiane on February 19, 2026.
STR / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Two Filipinos are currently the subjects of an ongoing investigation by the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) over their alleged link to a recent high-value drug bust in Laos, which authorities also confirmed was bound for the Philippines.

In a press briefing on Monday, October 12, the drug enforcement agency said they have established that the 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine, or shabu, that Lao authorities intercepted over a week ago at Luang Prabang International Airport was supposed to be delivered to the Philippines through a private jet.

The pilot of the private jet reportedly refused to load the luggage of the Filipino passenger who was carrying the luggage, which eventually led to the individual’s arrest and the plane’s cancellation of its flight to the Philippines.

“The very clear feature as of today is na-discover iyong droga dahil the pilot refused to load those baggages doon sa airplane papuntang Pilipinas. Kaya nung hindi na natuloy ‘yung ah 'yung pag-load ng baggages doon sa eroplano, ang ginawa ng airline company canceled its flight plan papunta sa Pilipinas,” PDEA Director General Undersecretary Isagani Nerez said.

(The very clear feature as of today is that the drugs were discovered because the pilot refused to load those baggages in the airplane bound for the Philippines. That's why the loading of baggage did not proceed, and the airline company canceled its flight going to the Philippines.)
The agency identified the arrested suspect as “Fajad”, a confirmed Filipino national with alleged current residence in Marawi. Nerez said they also have a list of Fajad’s other addresses.
Authorities are now investigating to identify Fajad’s accomplices while he remains detained in Laos, including another Filipino identified as “Boyet”.
'Boyet'
Nerez said Boyet is among the persons of interest in PDEA’s target list for allegedly being responsible for chartering the private jet that was supposed to be used to transport the suspected drugs.
The authorities said they have established a link between Fajad and Boyet, and found that both of them have residences in Luzon.
“We have a data that si Boyet is taga-rito sa Luzon, at ‘yung si Fajad meron ding address sa Luzon, parehas po. So that links them na or establish 'yung link nila na magkakilala,” Nerez said.
(We have data showing that Boyet is from Luzon, and Fajad also has an address in Luzon. So that links them or establishes a connection between them, suggesting that they know each other.)
Boyet allegedly paid for the private jet through bank transfer, but authorities did not disclose the amount.
PDEA also said they have acquired information saying Boyet had already skipped the country and went to Hong Kong.
The agency said they are currently building a case against both Boyet and Fajad, noting that some of the information remains confidential amid the probe.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial (October 13, 2026)
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will start at 1 p.m. on Tuesday, October 13, at the Senate impeachment court. Here are the latest news and updates.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 6:51am
Day 38 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Oct. 12, 2026. Senate
Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 39: What to expect
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday is set to tackle the manifestation of the House prosecution panel to drop Article III or the bribery charges in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero acknowledged on Monday the receipt of the October 6 manifestation by the prosecution, saying that the impeachment court is taking the matter “in advisement.”

“[The trial shall] resume tomorrow for the final manifestations to be made by the panel of prosecutors, as well as any other manifestations the parties wish to make, as well as administrative matters that the court need to address, if indeed the panel of prosecutors will persist in their intention to drop Article III and to rest all together,” Escudero said during the trial on Monday.
The impeachment court is set to resume the trial at 1 p.m. today.
The House prosecution has already presented three out of the four Articles of Impeachment originally filed against Duterte.

The first was Article IV or the alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez.
This was followed by Article I or the alleged misuse of confidential funds.
The prosecution on Monday finished with the presentation of evidence for Article II, pertaining to the allegation that the Vice President amassed millions in unexplained wealth.
The last witness the prosecution presented for its case-in-chief was financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera.

Should the prosecution rest its case today, it will be given time by the court to submit its formal offer of evidence in the impeachment trial. The defense is expected to comment on the matter. —Giselle Ombay/BAP/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Canada falls 4-3 to Denmark in women's soccer friendly in Toronto
articles.summary: Olivia Holdt scored twice and had an assist to lead Denmark to a 4-3 victory over Canada in a women's international soccer friendly on Monday at BMO Field in Toronto.

image.caption: Canada goalkeeper Kailen Sheridan, left, and teammate Janine Sonis react after Denmark's Olivia Holdt, not shown, scored her country's third goal during first half of Monday's international friendly at BMO Field in Toronto. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Soccer·New
Olivia Holdt scored twice and had an assist to lead Denmark to a 4-3 victory over Canada in a women's international soccer friendly on Monday at BMO Field in Toronto.
The teams played to a 1-1 draw on Friday in Montreal
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 12, 2026 6:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 12 minutes ago
Pernille Harder and Janni Thomsen also tallied for the visitors, who blitzed the hosts with three goals in a nine-minute span in the opening half.
Olivia Smith, Evelyne Viens and Delaney Pridham scored for Canada in front of an announced crowd of 12,112 on a warm, mostly sunny afternoon at the lakefront stadium.
The teams played to a 1-1 draw on Friday in Montreal. Smith scored a late equalizer for the hosts in that game and Canada won the unofficial shootout 4-2.

On Monday, the ninth-ranked Canadians started with a 4-2-3-1 formation while the 12th-ranked Danes went with a 3-4-3. Kailen Sheridan started in net for Canada and Jessie Fleming wore the captain's armband.
Canada comes up just short against Denmark in Toronto FIFA friendly

Pridham opened the scoring in the 10th minute after Kaylee Hunter headed the ball low into a packed penalty area. Pridham swiveled and beat goalkeeper Freja Thisgaard for her first goal with the women's senior team.
Canada kept the pressure on and was nearly rewarded moments later when Smith's shot from outside the area glanced off Thisgaard and hit the post.
Denmark scoring surge
Defensive miscues contributed to the Denmark scoring surge.

Holdt took possession of a loose ball after Canada's Julia Grosso couldn't corral a pass from defender Kadeisha Buchanan at midfield. The Danish forward took a few strides inside the halfway line and launched a shot that sailed over Sheridan's head and bounced into the net in the 24th minute.

An errant pass attempt by Buchanan moments later created another turnover. A strike from Sofie Bredgaard hit the crossbar but Denmark controlled the rebound and Harder beat Sheridan in the 27th minute.
In the 32nd minute, Ashley Lawrence's pass to Jade Rose was turned over down low and the ball found its way to an open Holdt, who earned her first international brace.
The tempo picked up in the second half as Pridham and Buchanan came off for Viens and Shelina Zadorsky.

Canada cut the deficit in the 49th minute after some heady work by Smith, who found Viens at the top of the area. Viens made a sliding shot attempt that deflected high off a defender and bounced off the grass and into the top corner.
Thomsen restored Denmark's two-goal cushion in the 61st minute as she coolly slotted a ball between two defenders and past Sheridan.
Smith scored from outside the box in the 70th minute. Her strike was misplayed by Thisgaard, who got down low to gather the ball but had it roll between her legs and over the line.
Casey Stoney is still seeking her first victory against a top-15 opponent since taking over as Canada's head coach in January 2025.
Upcoming CONCACAF W Championship
The friendlies served as a measuring stick ahead of Canada's opening match against No. 54 Panama at the CONCACAF W Championship on Nov. 28.

The tournament is a qualifier for both the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Denmark has already qualified for the World Cup after finishing atop its UEFA qualifying group.
Left back Allysha Chapman came on in the 89th minute for her 100th and final international appearance for Canada. She was feted during a ceremony after the game.

Fleming, Buchanan and Lawrence were honoured before the game for reaching 150 career international appearances. At halftime, Melissa Tancredi was acknowledged for her induction into the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame.
Canada fell to 3-4-1 in eight all-time meetings against Denmark.

articles.title: Emergency medical help for Christa Pike was delayed due to confusion, 911 tapes reveal
articles.summary: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings…

image.caption: 911 recordings suggest emergency care was delayed after the failed execution of Christa Pike, seen here in December 2007. (J. Miles Cary/ Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by The Associated Press.
First responders not sure whether request for emergency help in execution chamber was legitimate

The recordings show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate. The first call came in at 8:40 p.m. local time on Sept. 30, and it was about half an hour before prison officials affirmed it was legitimate and began letting responders through the prison gates.

"Per supervisors here at the DEC [Department of Emergency Communications], we have been informed it is a false call," one unidentified person says at 9:03 p.m. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison."

items: Tennessee governor orders outside review after death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt
After day of delays, witnesses say Tennessee unable to carry out execution of Christa Pike

blocks.text: Four minutes later, a responder reported: "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it's real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people."
It wasn't until 9:11 p.m. that prison officials affirmed the call for help was legitimate, the calls show.
Pike discharged from hospital

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point, Pike was on a ventilator, and her lawyers did not expect her to survive.

However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance, and she has since been discharged and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women's prison where she was housed for 30 years.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
