articles.title: Why the US is bringing back firing squads
articles.summary: Medical experts and those who study the death penalty say each method can go wrong and cause severe pain.

blocks.text: Warning: this story contains upsetting descriptions of executions
America's use of the death penalty is under the spotlight once again after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the military would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan.
The former military psychiatrist fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.
His execution would be the first time the US Army had used a firing squad since 1945, a method that several states already authorise to put people to death.
And it comes on the heels of the botched death by lethal injection of Christa Pike - a woman convicted of murdering her classmate.
Pike was taken to hospital and then discharged to prison 10 days later, after making a recovery from the failed attempt, her lawyers said.

Amid rising concerns over botched executions - and renewed federal support for the death penalty - the US has introduced both new and old forms of execution like firing squads, the electric chair and the gas chamber.
Lethal injection, which was first used in Texas in 1982, is now the most common way people are executed across the US, with many states making it their default method.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, said states turned to lethal injection because it appeared from the outside to be a more peaceful means of execution.
"That was a myth," he said.
Dr Zivot said that sometimes the injection of the drugs can cause pulmonary edema, when a person's lungs fill with fluid, which can give people the painful sensation of drowning.
"It's a terrifying way to die - to drown," he said.

Other times, people have medical conditions, like Pike - who suffered from thrombocytosis and other medical problems her lawyers warned about - that can complicate the execution and make it more painful.
During Pike's failed execution, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.
There are a host of reasons why so many lethal injections have been botched, but some of the same factors persist, said Maher.

"Oftentimes, the executions go wrong because training of staff is inadequate, because drugs are degraded or expired or improperly stored, or because states are experimenting with different combinations of drugs that have never been used before," she said.
In light of many of these challenges, some states have turned to executing people with a new and controversial method: nitrogen gas.
Alabama and Louisiana are the first states to have carried out executions with nitrogen gas, though three other states - Arkansas, Mississippi and Oklahoma - also allow for it.
Two years ago, Alabama used nitrogen gas to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith, after a botched attempt to put him to death via lethal injection in 2022.
During the execution, which took 25 minutes, Smith thrashed violently on the gurney as he was given the gas, a witness told the BBC at the time.
The method involves forcing a prisoner to breathe pure nitrogen gas until they suffocate.
Dr Zivot said people who breathe in the gas sometimes get seizures. Alabama has executed seven people using nitrogen gas since introducing the method in January 2024.
"Each time it was a horror show of struggling, of moving, of seizing," Dr Zivot said.
While some states have explored new methods, others have reauthorised some of the earliest ways US officials used to put people to death.
As of this year, nine states have approved execution by electric chair, with South Carolina using it as their default method.
Electrocution "has a horrible history of botched executions", Maher said, and errors with these executions is one of the reasons why states introduced lethal injections in the first place.
In 1997, Pedro Medina's head caught fire as he was put to death in an electric chair in Florida.
"A solid flame covered his whole head, from one side to the other. I had the impression of somebody being burned alive," his attorney Mike Minerva said, according to the Los Angeles Times.
A method once used as punishment in the military and in times of war, firing squad executions have also proven susceptible to human error.

Mikahl Mahdi was executed by a three-person firing squad last year after admitting to killing an off-duty police officer in 2004. But his lawyers say his death was prolonged because the bullets missed his heart and instead hit his liver and other organs.

In July, Idaho became the first state to use a firing squad as its primary method of execution after it ran into issues with lethal injections. Mississippi, Oklahoma, Utah and South Carolina also authorise this execution method.

Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan in the Fort Hood attack, told the BBC the firing squad was a "befitting" method to end his life because lethal injection and a gas chamber would be "doing him a favour".

Hanging was the main method of execution in the US until the 1890s, and several Asian countries including Japan and Singapore still use this method. But in the US, no states authorise hanging because of its "terrible" history, Maher said.
"Hanging has such a terrible association with racial violence and lynching in the states," she said. "So that is why there's no state that's using hanging or has authorised that method to be used."
Trump - a proponent of the death penalty - brought back the federal death penalty when he returned to office in 2025, after Joe Biden's administration put a moratorium on federal executions in 2021.

"Capital punishment is an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens," his office wrote in an executive order.
Maher said there has been "quite a bit of activity" in state legislatures to approve and reauthorise other methods of execution since Trump began expressing enthusiasm for the death penalty.

Trump has called for the death penalty to be expanded to punish large-scale drug dealers, human traffickers and those who kill police officers. Over the past 50 years, all prisoners who received death sentences were convicted of murder, though capital punishment was also used for rape convictions before that.

Asked by reporters whether Pike's failed lethal injection should spur changes to the death penalty, Trump did not directly answer the question, adding that the execution method "shouldn't be very difficult".

articles.title: Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
articles.summary: Despite securing key approvals, the Starlink satellite internet service remains in regulatory limbo, raising questions about security clearances, competition and India’s investment climate.

image.caption: Musk last week blamed unnamed Indian 'oligarchs' for delaying Starlink's launchImage: rokas91/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India. Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.
"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling."
A delayed launch and a war of words
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.

Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks. He said: "I have no comments to make. We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.
Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.
Its low-earth-orbit satellites could provide internet access in remote villages, hilly regions and border areas where fiber-optic networks and mobile towers are expensive to build.
But the service would enter a market where mobile data is inexpensive and established telecom operators have extensive networks.

blocks.caption: Musk said he would price Starlink's satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Ambani's low-cost Reliance Jio [FILE: February 13, 2025]Image: Pib/Press Information/Planet Pix/ZUMA Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: India's Ministry of Communications says security assessments for all three licensed satellite operators are under way and that they are at broadly the same regulatory stage.

In a statement, the ministry said every licensee must meet security conditions intended to protect users and their data. Once an assessment is completed, an operator can seek spectrum assignment. It described allegations that the framework was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived."
Legitimate security concerns?

Starlink secured a satellite communications licence from the Department of Telecommunications and authorization from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center in 2025. These approvals do not automatically permit commercial operations, however.

The security debate surrounding Starlink has intensified following remarks by BJP leader Nishikant Dubey, who chairs a parliamentary committee. In a post on X on October 11, Dubey said the panel had examined Starlink's security challenges.
"As the chairman of the parliamentary committee, our committee has understood the challenges facing the country's security agencies through Starlink," he wrote in Hindi language.
Responding to Musk's criticism, Dubey added: "India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation, and it does not change its security policy under pressure from social media or external figures."
Dubey did not specify the security risks or regulatory requirements holding up the launch.

blocks.caption: ​India is one of the world's biggest ‌internet markets [FILE: August 21, 2022]Image: Ashish Vaishnav/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former intelligence officer and national security expert Yashovardhan Jha Azad said the impasse reflected commercial competition, regulatory uncertainty and legitimate security concerns.
"The central question is: who retains effective control over an essential communications service during a crisis?" Azad told DW.
He said India needed safeguards covering traffic routing, lawful interception under due process and cybersecurity.

"The existence of security requirements, however, does not establish why Starlink's application remains pending," Azad said. He pointed out that the government has not publicly detailed which specific conditions, if any, the company still needs to satisfy.
Investment, manufacturing and affordability
The delay in Starlink's launch has raised questions about the predictability of India's investment environment.

Economist Lekha Chakrabarty, who has studied the issue closely, said the problem was not that India was shutting its doors to foreign investment, but that companies could not plan around an open-ended approval process.
"The Starlink impasse is best read not as India closing its door to foreign investment, but as a failure to make an already open door predictably passable," Chakrabarty told DW.
She said security reviews were necessary given the sensitivity of satellite communications, which involve critical infrastructure, cross-border data, gateway control and lawful interception.
But the problem, she said, was the lack of transparency around approval criteria and timelines.
"Investors can price known rules, they cannot efficiently price discretionary, multi-agency processes with uncertain endpoints," Chakrabarty added.
World seeks wider web as US dominates satellite internet

Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association, said Starlink's entry could create opportunities for Indian electronics manufacturers in satellite terminals, antennas, communication modules and network equipment.

"India already has a strong trusted electronics manufacturing base, which provides an opportunity for global technology companies to develop local partnerships and strengthen domestic supply chains," he told DW.

articles.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
articles.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

blocks.text: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers reportedly gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.
The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.
Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
Some supermarket staff reportedly said they were hit by waves of hot air when they opened freezer units on Monday morning.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it had opened an investigation into the incident, which it called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

Eoropean Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
The full scale of the attack is so far unclear.

Reports in specialist retail and local media said stores from other food giants, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, were also attacked. BBC News has approached the supermarket chains for comment.
In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

articles.title: Robin Padilla questions Cabrera's former firm ties; Diokno expresses full trust in witness
articles.summary: Senator-judge Robin Padilla on Monday questioned financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera over his former accounting firm"s ties to a company facing complaints allegedly involving billions of…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 10:29pm

Senator-judge Robin Padilla on Monday questioned financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera over his former accounting firm’s ties to a company facing complaints allegedly involving billions of pesos.
Despite this, House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno reaffirmed his full trust in the witness during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.
During his interjection on Day 38, Padilla asked Diokno if he knew that the prosecution witness worked in Isla Lipana & Co.

The senator-judge said that this company supposedly vouched that MFT Group of Companies---a firm that faced criminal complaints and a cease and desist order from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)---was “financially healthy.”

“Meron pong reklamo dito sa company na ito na ito raw ay nang-biktima ng mga OFW na maraming bouncing checks at isinabit nitong MFT Group of Companies na umaabot sa P5 bilyon. Ang tanong ko po, hindi niyo po ba alam na ‘yung Isla Lipana ang independent auditor nitong MFT Group of Companies?” Padilla asked.

(There are complaints against the MFT Group of Companies regarding the victimization of OFWs through bouncing checks and liabilities amounting to P5 billion. My question is, were you not aware that Isla Lipana is the independent auditor for the MFT Group of Companies?)
Diokno then distanced Cabrera from the issue.
“Ang alam ko po ay itong MFT Group of Companies ay hindi kasama sa mga kasong ito ang ating testigo, si Atty. Alex Cabrera,” Diokno said.
(As far as I know, our witness, Atty. Alex Cabrera, is not included in these cases of the MFT Group of Companies.)
Padilla asked Cabrera if he became chairman of Isla Lipana & Co. The witness answered in the affirmative, saying he served as the firm’s top official from 2013 to 2021.
Cabrera also confirmed he is familiar with the MFT Group of Companies.
“Sa 104 years of existence namin, ngayon lang kami nadamay sa ganyang uri ng problema… ‘Yung kaso po nung nangyari po ay tapos na ang aking term,” he said.
(In our 104 years of existence, this is the first time we’ve been dragged into that kind of problem… My term had already ended when those cases were filed.)
Padilla went back to Diokno to ask if the prosecution was okay with the supposed tainted image of Isla Lipana under the chairmanship of Cabrera.
Diokno said that his trust in the witness remains steady. “Buong-buo po ang tiwala ko kay Atty, Cabrera,” he said.
(I have complete trust in Atty. Cabrera.)

“Ang pagkaintindi ko po sa kasong ‘yan, ang naging kliyente ng Isla Lipana ay ‘yung parent company lang po at ang alam ko, ‘yung nagka-problema na nabanggit niyo Sen. Robin, ay involved the subsidiaries who were not engaged by or who were not served by Isla Lipana,” he added.
(From my understanding, Isla Lipana’s client was only the parent company, and the issue you mentioned, Senator Robin, involved subsidiaries that were not engaged by or served by Isla Lipana.)
Appeal to the court
In his interjection, Padilla also underscored the importance of fairness in the trial and not rushing the impeachment proceedings.

“Sa amin naman po, gagawin din namin ang trabaho namin na hindi namin ito mamadaliin. Hindi rin po kami magkukulang sa oras at hihingin po namin sa aming Senate President at sa aming tagapamahalang hukom na ‘wag nating madaliin ito dahil itong bagay na ‘to, nakasalalay dito ang 32 million votes ng taumbayan,” he said.

(We will also do our job without rushing the impeachment proceedings. We will not cut it short and we will ask our Senate President and the presiding officer not to rush it, because the 32 million votes of the people hinge on this matter.)
Padilla also briefly asked Cabrera if it is true that he met with former vice president and incumbent Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo in December 2025.
“Tama po (that’s correct),” the witness answered. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
articles.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV had only recently returned from a trip to France when he announced doctors had found a nodule on his lungImage: Grzegorz Galazka/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.
At under 3 cm (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.
In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.
What we know so far
All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."
That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.
Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

At the same time, the risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules." That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.
Fortunately, however, many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.
It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.
What are lung nodules?
Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.
Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.
Causes and symptoms of lung nodules
Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.
At more than 3 cm, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.
What makes lung nodules cancerous?
It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.
At 2 mm or smaller the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 mm.
The risk of cancer becomes 9-10% at about 8 to 10 mm. And at larger than 1 cm, the risk of cancer is about 15%.
The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.
There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.
According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."
A journey through lung health
Lung nodules and lung cancer are common
It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."
However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

articles.title: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
articles.summary: Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.

blocks.text: US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said but no further details were given.
Omar was born in Somalia and came to the US aged eight fleeing war. First elected to Congress in 2018, she is running for reelection next month, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home. The BBC has contacted Omar for comment.

While the nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time her immigration records have been scrutinised by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.

Omar, a Democrat, has been the target of Trump's insults and the president previously suggested that she "should go back" to Somalia and at times said she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as "unhealthy and creepy obsession."

The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."

Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.

articles.title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: Shadrack Sibiya had denied grooming a 16-year-old and raping an 18-year-old.

blocks.text: South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking.
Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied.
Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.

The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

articles.title: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme
articles.summary: US officials had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to Álvaro Pulido's arrest.

blocks.text: A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States.

The US Department of Justice said Álvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody.
Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest.
He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office.
Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court.

The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes".
US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine.
They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US.
They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida.
Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024.
However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed.
Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US.
Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

articles.title: Fugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery case
articles.summary:
A businessman wanted in the US for allegedly bribing top Venezuelan officials has been taken into custody

A businessman wanted for years in the

blocks.text: A businessman wanted for years in the US for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.

Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the state department had been offering a reward of up to $10m for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido, 62, was taken into US custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agencies, American officials said on Sunday.
It was unclear how Pulido ended up in US custody. He was scheduled to make his initial court appearance on Tuesday in Miami.

“His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, wrote in a social media post Sunday.

“No amount of time or distance will stop” the justice department “from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom,” he wrote.

Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge that Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the US, sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.

The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro’s vice-president. She took over as Venezuela’s acting president following the US military’s ouster of Maduro in January.

Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for more than $2bn in contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.

Prior to these alleged offenses, Pulido had a prolific history of drug trafficking, including a 1997 conviction in Italy under the alias of German Enrique Rubio, the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Florida said in a statement.

Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the US by Rodríguez in May. In September, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195m in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.

articles.title: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
articles.summary: Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.

image.caption: Zelenskyy's POW revelation at the UN has caused a major rift with SeoulImage: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.

The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.

The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.
Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.
Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.

Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.
The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.
Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine
What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy?
There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.
"The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said.

"Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North."

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

"There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.
"I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said.
Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy
Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired?
While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.
Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.
Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue.

"Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said.
"I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."

articles.title: B.C. man reunited with beloved flute, 5 years after it floated away down a Yukon river
articles.summary: Jun Takahashi was stunned when he saw the online post: someone in the Yukon bush had found a canoe barrel full of his mildew-y camping gear, and his long-lost flute.

image.caption: Jun Takahashi of B.C., on a canoe trip in the Yukon in June 2021. Takahashi and his paddling partner flipped their boat during that trip, losing their gear — and Takahashi's beloved flute. (Submitted by Jun Takahashi)

blocks.text: North
Jun Takahashi was stunned when he saw the online post: someone in the Yukon bush had found a canoe barrel full of his mildew-y camping gear, and his long-lost flute.
Jun Takahashi had wondered if some bear in Alaska was now playing it
Jun Takahashi was stunned when he saw the post on social media.
"Like, what? Like, I couldn't believe it," he said, from his home on Salt Spring Island, B.C.

The post on a Yukon paddling group page was by someone who had recently found a blue, waterproof canoe barrel full of camping gear, near the confluence of a couple of remote Yukon rivers. The poster, Colin Abbott, asked if anybody had dumped in Yukon's Kathleen River "in the last couple of years" and might be missing their gear.
There was also a picture, showing the blue barrel, some clothes and a sleeping bag strewn across a floor — and, in the middle, a flute in a case.
Colin Abbott posted this photo on social media after he found the barrel full of gear last month. (Colin Abbott)
Takahashi recognized it immediately. The flute meant a lot to him — he'd bought in Japan years ago and had carried it with him on his many travels.

It was the perfect thing to travel with, especially on a remote canoe trip in the Yukon. It could be easily stuffed inside one of those waterproof barrels for your gear. Takahashi also loved to play it in wild, open spaces.
"Like, I don't disturb anybody," he said.
Takahashi likes to play his flute in remote places where he won't disturb anyone. (Submitted by Jun Takahashi)
Before last week, he'd assumed he would never see the instrument again.

He lost it in June 2021, when he and a friend were on a canoe trip down the Kathleen River and accidentally flipped their boat. It was a scramble to escape the frigid water with their lives, so the canoe and their gear had to be left to be swept down the fast-moving river.
In the following days, the two took to social media asking any paddlers to keep an eye out for their gear and even offered a cash reward.
Takahashi and Sonia Lévêque on their ill-fated canoe trip in 2021. (Submitted by Jun Takahashi)
Takahashi thought the lost barrel might be adrift somewhere on the Bering Sea by now. Or, he imagined an "Alaskan bear wearing my down jacket or like, playing my flute or something."
'Someone would know this story'
It turns out the barrel, and all of its contents, had not travelled that far.
Abbott says he found it last month near the confluence of the Kathleen and Dezadeash Rivers. He was tracking a moose in the bush when he spotted a "patch of blue" near an opening.
It wasn't a completely surprising find. Abbott has paddled the Kathleen River himself and seen wrecked boats and other remnants of river mishaps.
Colin Abbott says when he found the gear and the flute, he 'figured that someone would know this story.' (Submitted by Colin Abbott)
He cracked the blue barrel open a bit to ensure it wasn't full of rotten food. Then he took it home to fully unpack as "a surprise for myself and my partner and my roommates."
The camping gear and clothing were a bit mildew-y, but the most interesting thing was the flute, still safely in its case.
"I figured that someone would know this story, but I wasn't sure," Abbott recalled.
That's when he posted the photo online — and soon heard from Takahashi.
Now, a Yukon friend of Takahashi will bring the flute and the other gear with him next time he travels to B.C.
Takahashi is delighted to be getting his beloved, well-travelled instrument back.
"I like playing flute in the nature. That's a good practice," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Paul Tukker is a writer and reporter with CBC News in Whitehorse. Before moving to Yukon in 2014, he worked with CBC in Sudbury and Iqaluit. You can reach him at paul.tukker@cbc.ca.
With files from George Maratos

articles.title: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees
articles.summary:
Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s…

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.

blocks.caption: NAZA’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival last month. Photograph: Capital Pictures/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.
The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

blocks.caption: Graffiti depicting Abraham and Szor, and the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, appeared on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel, after NAZA was awarded the special jury prize at the Venice film festival.  Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

articles.title: Cyprus closer than ever to joining Schengen but political hurdles relating to the Green Line and British Sovereign Base Areas remain
articles.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's…

image.caption: There are nine designated crossing points between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island. Pictured here: the Leda Street crossing point in NicosiaImage: Mpalis/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

blocks.caption: Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countriesImage: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

blocks.caption: The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP)Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

blocks.caption: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the islandImage: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia launched strikes hours after Donald Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire'
articles.summary: Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes on the northeastern city of Kharkiv. The Kremlin says it would only consider a one-day…

image.caption: At least 12 people were reportedly injured in Russian strikes on Kharkiv, according to the city's mayorImage: Andrii Marienko/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend.
Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."
There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."
Ukrainian energy facility attacked

On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.
"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
Zelenskyy: Ukraine 'will respond' if no ceasefire
Zelenskyy expressed readiness in principle to back an agreement to refrain from attacks on energy infrastructure, but said such a ceasefire must be backed up by security guarantees.
"This ceasefire, it can work, and it can ​become ⁠a major step toward ending the war if ⁠the ​Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said.
"We are waiting for the ​of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to ​see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.
"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."

French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."
The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.
The Kremlin earlier rejected ​a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by ⁠President ​Zelenskyy.
"I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.summary:
Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breach stretched defences

Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh on Monday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one dead.

The Gulf nation said it was taking the step after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.

King Khalid international airport was being kept closed to complete verification of the airport’s safety, the Saudi aviation authority said. Saudi Arabia’s military spokesperson also said further missile and drone threats had been detected.

blocks.caption: Before and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday. Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters

blocks.text: The closure came as the country pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises.

An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.

The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014.

Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi air planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.

The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.

Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids through Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.

blocks.caption: A billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.

The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.

The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.

Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.

Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

articles.title: Tom Cruise film Digger could lose $245m at box office
articles.summary: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.

blocks.text: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance in cinemas.
Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend.
It brings Digger's total box office takings to around $35m (£26m) globally so far. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".
The film's takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.
Digger's performance is in sharp contrast to the success of IP-driven hits starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of the Top Gun and Mission: Impossible franchises.
Digger is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.
Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.
The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.
However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).
Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

articles.title: Half Canadian, half American: the high school football team showcasing cross-border co-operation
articles.summary: It’s not many high school athletes that need to bring a passport to practice. But that’s the case for a group of young football players in southern Alberta, who, during a time of heightened political…

image.caption: For the first time, six players from Milk River, Alta., are crossing the border to play football with the high school team in Sunburst, Mont. (Joshua Mclean/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

It’s not many high school athletes that need to bring a passport to practice. But that’s the case for a group of young football players in southern Alberta, who, during a time of heightened political tensions between Canada and the U.S., are now playing for an American high school team.
Program between Alberta and Montana schools believed to be first of its kind
It’s not many high school athletes that need to bring a passport to practice.

But that’s the case for a group of young football players in southern Alberta, who, during a time of heightened political tensions between Canada and the U.S., are now playing for an American high school team.
The high school in Milk River, Alta. — a town with a population of less than 1,000 people — isn’t large enough for a football team of its own.
And going into the school year, the Sunburst Refiners, in a town just south of the border in Montana, had only seven players of their own — not enough to play six-man football for a whole season.
Enter the idea for some cross-border co-operation, believed to be a first-of-its-kind program.

“It’s sure been a pretty crazy challenge uniting them and just bringing them together, and just seeing it all come together and how well the kids have meshed has been pretty fun,” said Scotty Bye, the Refiners' head coach.
The Sunburst Refiners (in red) play against the Heart Butte Warriors in a snowy game on Saturday, Oct. 10. Sunburst won 53-0. (Joshua Mclean/CBC)
Part of that challenge, he says, has been getting players up to speed who have never played on a high school football team, and may have had limited experience with the game itself.
Even for those who had played before, six-man football comes with its own differences. The field is smaller, there are some different rules and penalties, and scores can run much higher.
Near-daily trips across the border
Getting to the field in Montana takes a bit of extra work.
The Canadian players go down almost daily for games or after-school practices, meaning they’ve already crossed the border what one player estimates to be about 100 times.
Crossing by foot speeds the process up, Bye says, with the players able to skip to the front of the line rather than wait in idling vehicles.

Parents have organized carpools to take the players to the crossing, where they’ll get out and walk across the border. Once past, they’ll wait for a bus that comes to pick them up and bring them to the field.
A sign welcomes visitors to the town of Sunburst, Mont. (Joshua Mclean/CBC)
Players might travel as far as four hours into Montana for away games, and have been told next year they’ll likely play a game eight hours away.
Before the start of the season, grade 10 student Brennus Vengroff says border agents did a walkthrough with the players, to get them used to the process.
He says the only issues that have come up have been a player forgetting their passport, and having to double back for it. But for the most part, the process has been smooth.
How Alberta students ended up playing on a U.S. high school’s football team
“A lot of the [border] agents are familiar with the boys and expect that they're going to be there every day after school,” said Julie Vengroff, Brennus’ mom.
Her husband, Adam Vengroff, says Sunburst almost feels like an extension of their own community.
“The border is almost non-existent. If it wasn't for the Border Patrol itself, it would be pretty much just like driving to another small town in Canada,” he said.
O Canada
The team has made some nods to its Canadian contingent, like playing O Canada before every home game.
The team's booster club designed sweartshirts for the team, including one with Refiners’ logo flanked by both the Canadian and American flags. Beneath it reads “Two Countries, One Team.”
Coach Bye says aside from maybe some differences in accents, you’d never be able to tell which player is from which country.
“It looks like they've been hanging around each other for 10 years,” Bye said. “The culture I would almost say is no different.”
The Refiners now play O Canada before every home game, in honour of their six Canadian teammates. (Joshua Mclean/CBC)
He added that part of the joy is watching everyone come together, including parents and other Milk River residents, who will watch the game and then go downtown to hang out together after.
It’s cool to see, he said, given “all the crap you see in politics.”
Grade 11 player Jett Butler says at first, he was a bit nervous to join the team.
“Because I didn't know if they would like us or not, but yeah, it's pretty fun. So, glad I did it,” said Butler, who recently scored his first touchdown.
Bye says one regret is that the program didn’t start even sooner: with more time to train up the players, he thinks about how well the team could be doing now.
But he’s encouraged that the excitement seems to be extending to younger players who’ve already expressed interest in playing for the team one day.
“This isn't a one-and-done thing, right? We want this to sustain and be the future of our football program,” said Bye.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca
With files from Sheehan Desjardins and Joshua Mclean

articles.title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
articles.summary: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
articles.byline: Ed Walton and James Parrish for MetDesk

blocks.text: Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.

An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.

In Kosanica, Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.

Elsewhere in Europe, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.

Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.

Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.

blocks.caption: People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.

At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.

Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia
articles.summary: The European Union has approved its largest-ever sanctions package against Moscow, targeting more than 1,000 entities tied to the military-industrial complex.

image.caption: Businesses and individuals tied to missile production were named in this group of sanctions in particularImage: Alexei Konovalov/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
Who do the sanctions target?
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.

"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
What is the latest development in the war?
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.

US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.
